A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete text, equations, figures and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original graph-planning experiments measuring accuracy, output diversity and learned graph structure on Erdős–Rényi graphs and a graph abstraction of Blocksworld.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original attention analyses for one- and two-layer transformers in Appendix G.1.

M1.justification: The SFT, PG and Q-learning procedures, losses and reward designs remain unchanged. Separating source/target token names and shifting path indices is equivalent notation; the two-layer experiment adds a validation configuration rather than a proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 100-node Erdős–Rényi setting and four-block, 73-node Blocksworld graph. The new running example and attention study introduce no additional dataset, task or environment.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain SFT/continual SFT, PG with the same KL variants, and Q-learning with the same reward and sampling variants. The attention study examines existing methods without introducing a new comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix G.1 adds a two-layer, single-head configuration and an evaluation protocol measuring average attention at training checkpoints. Existing graph construction, splits, decoding settings and accuracy/diversity evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix G.1 directly investigates the central target/current-node assumption through attention dynamics under SFT, unregularized PG and process-reward Q-learning, including a two-layer extension. This adds a substantial mechanistic validation absent from v1.

E5.justification: Existing shaded variability displays are retained. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests or new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figures 5–6 newly report attention patterns, including SFT target-attention peaking then declining, stronger late-training concentration under RL, and target/current-node emphasis in two-layer models. Matched accuracy, diversity and graph-structure results are retained; v1 Figures 5–6 become v2 Figures 7–8.

T1.justification: The mathematical assumptions, theorem conclusions and derivations are retained after matching equivalent token notation. Theorem 5.1 corrects an assumption reference, and Appendix E.2 explains existing maximization equalities without changing the proof's mathematical content.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the outcome-reward Q-learning failure from reward hacking to Q-value bias, changing its stated diagnosis. The principal claims about SFT memorization, exploration, PG diversity collapse and process-reward Q-learning remain unchanged.

C2.justification: Appendix G.1 newly hypothesizes that declining target attention during SFT reflects overfitting and auxiliary prediction strategies. It interprets the attention results as support for the target/current-node abstraction across the tested architectures.

D1.justification: v2 specifies how attention is averaged over eligible SFT paths, the path-length condition for each row, and the restriction to the first eight rows. The reproducibility statement and supplementary-code availability statement are unchanged.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work discussion are unchanged. The running example reuses an already cited Blocksworld reference, without revising novelty claims or positioning relative to prior research.

P1.justification: v2 adds a Blocksworld running example, clearer source/target notation, explanatory proof prose and an attention-analysis subsection. Most existing prose and the overall section organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Two multi-panel attention figures are added. Existing figures are re-rendered or repositioned, and the earlier appendix plots are renumbered 7–8; their panel structures and scientific content are retained.

improvement.justification: The new attention study supplies direct empirical support for the central modeling abstraction in the tested small transformers. The running example, clearer notation and expanded proof explanation improve accessibility. These are useful, limited gains: the core theory, task coverage and performance evidence remain unchanged.
